method: Deterministic summary of computed figures. No language model is used.
national: One Nation led national search interest in the week to 19 October, averaging 24.3 on Google's 0-100 scale, 3.8 times the next party (the Greens). That is 63% of all search interest across the parties tracked.
The Greens rose the most on the previous week, up 2.9 points (+80%); One Nation fell furthest, down 4.9 points (-17%).

Searches for One Nation jumped to 53 on 19 October, 2.6 times the previous week's average. Coverage around that day: “PM, Coalition and crossbench support Jacqui Lambie after Pauline Hanson cartoon mocked vaginal prolapse” (The Guardian).

Searches for the Greens jumped to 18 on 15 October, 5.5 times the previous week's average. Coverage around that day: “Shoebridge says Greens taking allegations against senator 'incredibly seriously' — as it happened” (ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation).
Fastest-rising searches alongside One Nation: “mike newman”, “mike newman one nation”, “one nation immigration policy dispute”.
victoria: 38 days until Victorians vote on Saturday 28 November 2026.

Across the latest poll from each of 3 pollsters, the Coalition averages 29.0% of the primary vote, Labor 24.3%, One Nation 23.0% and the Greens 15.0%. On two-party-preferred the Coalition leads 54.5 to 45.5 (2 polls), a 9.5-point swing to the Coalition since 2022.
Applied uniformly to the 2022 pendulum, that swing points to a Coalition majority (55 seats, 45 needed). Treat this as the classic two-party read only: it cannot see One Nation winning seats.
The Roy Morgan MRP (March 2026 - September 2026), which models seats one by one, projects Coalition 62, Labor 40, One Nation 11 and Greens 6: a majority.
Preferred premier (Resolve, 6–10 Oct 2026): Wilson 29%, Carroll 22%, Pickering 14%.
